concepts.explanation: The interface encodes two different things on the same text. Background color shows the feature's activation at each token. Underline color shows the change in predicted log-likelihood of that token when the feature was ablated. In the paper's worked example, a feature active on token [B] in the sequence [A][B][C] whose ablation reduces the odds placed on [C] produces an orange background on [B] and a blue underline on [C] — meaning ablation increased the model's loss on [C], so the feature was helping predict it. Keeping activation and effect on separate visual channels is what lets a reader see the offset between where a feature fires and where it pays off.

concepts.name: Feature Interpretability Rubric
concepts.summary: A scored checklist a human follows to rate how interpretable a feature is, summing to a maximum of 14 points.
concepts.explanation: The rater first forms an interpretation of the feature from its positive logits and its activations across all intervals, then scores five things: confidence in that interpretation (0–3), how consistent the high-activation bolded tokens are with it (0–5), how consistent the positive logit effects are with it (0–3), whether inconsistent logit effects were at least separated in effect size from the consistent ones (0 or 1), and how specific the interpretation is (0–3). The total is the sum. The maximum is 14 rather than 15 because a perfect score on the logit-consistency item makes the separation item inapplicable.

concepts.name: Interpretation Before Scoring
concepts.summary: The rater commits to an interpretation first, then scores the evidence against it — rather than scoring interpretability in the abstract.
concepts.explanation: Every item after the first is phrased relative to 'your interpretation from (1)', so the rubric measures whether a specific hypothesis holds up rather than asking for a global impression. This makes the score sensitive to how the rater chose to describe the feature: a vague interpretation is easy to make consistent but scores low on specificity, while a sharp one risks inconsistency. The specificity item is what stops the rubric from rewarding interpretations broad enough to fit anything.

concepts.name: Effect-Size Separation Item
concepts.summary: A one-point item awarded when inconsistent positive logit effects are at least clearly smaller than the consistent ones.
concepts.explanation: A feature whose logit effects mostly match the interpretation but include some that do not is in a different position depending on whether the mismatched effects are large or negligible. This item gives one point when there was a separation in effect size between the consistent and inconsistent effects, and zero otherwise or when not applicable. It is the item that becomes inapplicable — and so caps the total at 14 rather than 15 — when the logit consistency score is already perfect.

concepts.name: Feature UMAPs
concepts.summary: Two-dimensional embeddings of the learned features, built from their decoder columns, used to look at how features are arranged relative to each other.
concepts.explanation: The paper represents each feature as the 512-dimensional column it occupies in the decoder matrix $W_d$ and embeds those vectors into two dimensions. The first embedding covers features from runs A/0 and A/1 jointly with n_neighbors=15, metric="cosine", min_dist=0.05. The second uses the same settings with min_dist=0.01 and also includes A/2. Embedding features from different-sized dictionaries into one map is what makes it possible to see where a coarse feature sits relative to the finer features it splits into.

concepts.name: UMAP
concepts.summary: A dimensionality reduction method that places high-dimensional points in two dimensions while trying to preserve local neighborhood structure.
concepts.explanation: UMAP builds a graph connecting each point to its nearest neighbors under some metric and then finds a low-dimensional layout that keeps those neighborhoods intact. Two settings matter for reading the paper's plots: n_neighbors=15 fixes how much local structure is preserved versus global, and min_dist controls how tightly points may be packed together in the output — the paper uses 0.05 and 0.01, both quite tight. The metric is cosine, so features are compared by direction rather than by magnitude, which is what you want given that dictionary columns are unit norm. Distances in a UMAP plot should be read as suggestive of neighborhood, not as faithful measurements.

concepts.name: HDBSCAN Clustering of Features
concepts.summary: Clusters shown on the first UMAP come from running HDBSCAN on a separate 10-dimensional UMAP embedding of the same features.
concepts.explanation: Rather than clustering the 2D plot, which would inherit its distortions, the paper fits a separate 10-dimensional UMAP of the same features with n_neighbors=15, metric="cosine", min_dist=0.1 and runs HDBSCAN on that with min_cluster_size=3. HDBSCAN is a density-based clustering method that finds clusters of varying density and leaves points in sparse regions unassigned, so it does not force every feature into a group. The minimum cluster size of 3 means even very small feature families can be picked out.

concepts.name: One-Dimensional Ordering of Features
concepts.summary: The feature list is sorted by a one-dimensional UMAP fit to the unclustered features together with the cluster medoids.
concepts.explanation: To put the feature list in a sensible linear order, the paper fits a one-dimensional UMAP over the features HDBSCAN left unclustered plus one representative — the medoid — for each cluster. Sorting by that coordinate puts similar features and similar clusters near each other in the list. Using medoids rather than every clustered feature keeps a large cluster from dominating the ordering.

flags.refText: Chen, Xi et al. Infogan: Interpretable representation learning by information maximizing generative adversarial nets. NeurIPS
flags.whyNeeded: The second concrete disentanglement method cited; the mutual-information objective over a subset of latent factors is the mechanism being described.

flags.refText: Yun, Zeyu et al. Transformer visualization via dictionary learning. arXiv:2103.15949
flags.whyNeeded: The prior state of the art for dictionary learning on transformer activations, and the undercomplete result this paper's overcomplete expansion is defined against.

flags.refText: Leo Gao et al. (2020). The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling.
flags.whyNeeded: The training corpus for both transformers; its composition directly determines which features exist (IRC, PLoS citations, license headers) and is required to reproduce the results.

flags.refText: Nanda, Neel, Lee, Andrew and Wattenberg, Martin. Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models. arXiv:2309.00941
flags.whyNeeded: The resolution of the apparent counterexample to features-as-directions; the alternative interpretation is what restores the linear representation hypothesis the paper's whole method assumes.

flags.refText: Li, Kenneth et al. Emergent world representations: Exploring a sequence model trained on a synthetic task. arXiv:2210.13382
flags.whyNeeded: The apparent counterexample itself; knowing what was found and why it looked non-linear is needed to judge the exchange the paper treats as an update on the hypothesis.

flags.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2021). A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Transformer Circuits Thread
flags.whyNeeded: The claim that a one-layer attention-only model can be analyzed without touching hidden states — and that a ReLU MLP blocks this — rests on the rewriting technique developed there.

flags.refText: Kaplan, Jared et al. Scaling laws for neural language models. arXiv:2001.08361
flags.whyNeeded: The template for the kind of empirical law the authors say they want for dictionary learning; what such laws predict and how they are fitted is assumed known.

flags.refText: Coenen, Andy et al. Visualizing and measuring the geometry of BERT. NeurIPS
flags.whyNeeded: Cited as the precedent for token-sense-in-context structure and the source of the German/English 'die' example used to argue some token-in-context features are intuitive.

flags.refText: Olah, Chris et al. (2020). Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits. Distill
flags.whyNeeded: One of the two sources for the universality claim as a research question, and for the circuits framing of features and their connections that the paper's goals are stated in.

flags.refText: Bricken, Trenton et al. Emergence of Sparse Representations from Noise.
flags.whyNeeded: The claim that noise injection increases interpretability by a route separate from an L1 penalty is a concrete suggested improvement to the method; the mechanism is not described here.

flags.refText: Olshausen, Bruno A and Field, David J (1997). Sparse coding with an overcomplete basis set: A strategy employed by V1?. Vision research
flags.whyNeeded: Section 2.4 rests its entire motivation for seeking a sparse overcomplete decomposition on this paper, pointing the reader at its 'Why Sparseness?' section rather than restating the argument. It is also one of the two citations that define sparse dictionary learning for the paper.

flags.refText: Elad, Michael (2010). Sparse and redundant representations: from theory to applications in signal and image processing.
flags.whyNeeded: The formal statement of the sparse dictionary learning problem — what is being optimized, over what — is deferred to this reference. Section 2.4 names the problem and moves on.

flags.refText: Elhage, Nelson and Hume, Tristan and Olsson, Catherine and Schiefer, Nicholas et al. (2022). Toy Models of Superposition. Transformer Circuits Thread
flags.whyNeeded: Section 2.4 uses this work's result — that many sparse features can live as directions in a lower-dimensional space — as the premise for the whole method. Sections 2.5.1 and 18.1 then rely on its toy models as the ground-truth evaluation setting and as the source of the 'bounce plots' diagnostic that motivated the pre-encoder bias, neither of which is described here.

flags.refText: Lee Sharkey and Dan Braun and Beren Millidge (2022). [Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders.
flags.whyNeeded: Section 2.4 describes its method as 'similar to Sharkey, et al.' This is the prior version of the sparse-autoencoder-for-superposition approach; knowing what it does is what makes this paper's modifications legible as modifications.

flags.refText: Aharon, Michal and Elad, Michael and Bruckstein, Alfred (2006). K-SVD: An algorithm for designing overcomplete dictionaries for sparse representation. IEEE Transactions on signal processing
flags.whyNeeded: K-SVD is one of the two named classical methods the paper says it tried and rejected as possibly 'too strong'. Assessing that argument requires knowing how iterative dictionary learning actually recovers codes.

flags.refText: Engan, Kjersti and Aase, Sven Ole and Husoy, J Hakon (1999). Method of optimal directions for frame design. ICASSP 1999
flags.whyNeeded: The other named classical alternative. Together with K-SVD it defines the baseline the sparse autoencoder is chosen over, and neither is described in this paper.

flags.refText: Leo Gao, Stella Biderman, Sid Black, Laurence Golding et al. (2020). The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling.
flags.whyNeeded: The Pile is both the transformer's training corpus and the source of the 40 million contexts for the autoencoder dataset. Its composition determines which features exist at all — base64, DNA and Arabic script features are corpus artifacts — and the paper explicitly warns some features are idiosyncratic to the dataset.

flags.refText: Kingma, Diederik P and Ba, Jimmy. Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. arXiv:1412.6980
flags.whyNeeded: Section 18.5's gradient-projection fix and section 18.3's optimizer state reset both turn on how Adam's per-parameter moment estimates accumulate from past gradients. Neither modification can be understood without that mechanism.

flags.refText: He, Kaiming and Zhang, Xiangyu and Ren, Shaoqing and Sun, Jian. Delving deep into rectifiers: Surpassing human-level performance on imagenet classification. ICCV
flags.whyNeeded: The autoencoder's initialization scheme is given only by name, and it also serves as the losing baseline in the neuron resampling comparison. The distribution and scaling are a reproduction detail defined only in the cited work.

flags.refText: Hobbhahn, Marius (2023). More findings on Memorization and double descent.
flags.whyNeeded: Section 18.1 says the pre-encoder bias investigation was motivated by Hobbhahn's observations but does not say what those observations were. The paper ranks this modification first in importance, so the justification matters.

flags.refText: Cunningham, Hoagy and Ewart, Aidan and Smith, Logan and Huben, Robert and Sharkey, Lee. Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Model Directions. arXiv:2309.08600
flags.whyNeeded: Cited in section 18.2 as establishing the tied-weight convention this paper departs from, and in 7.3 as evidence the approach scales. The comparison in 18.2 only means something against the details of their setup.

flags.refText: Alireza Makhzani and Brendan J. Frey (2013). k-Sparse Autoencoders. CoRR
flags.whyNeeded: The second citation for the tied-weight convention, and a different route to sparsity in autoencoders (a hard top-k constraint rather than an L1 penalty), which contextualizes this paper's choice of an L1 objective.

flags.refText: Frankle, Jonathan and Carbin, Michael. The lottery ticket hypothesis: Finding sparse, trainable neural networks. arXiv:1803.03635
flags.whyNeeded: Section 18.3 offers this hypothesis as the possible mechanism behind why neuron resampling works. The hypothesis's actual content and evidence are entirely in the cited paper.

flags.refText: Bricken, Trenton and Schaeffer, Rylan and Olshausen, Bruno and Kreiman, Gabriel. Emergence of Sparse Representations from Noise.
flags.whyNeeded: Section 18.3 says its findings on what causes dead neurons agree with this work but reproduces neither the experiments nor the mechanism. The list of causes — learning rate, batch size, dataset redundancy, step count, optimizer — is presented as corroborated rather than demonstrated here.

flags.refText: Smith, Logan (2023). (tentatively) Found 600+ Monosemantic Features in a Small LM Using Sparse Autoencoders.
flags.whyNeeded: Section 2.6 acknowledges that the one-layer model's near-linear logit structure may make its results less likely to generalize, and leans on this and two companion posts as the counterweight. The strength of that reassurance depends entirely on what those results actually show.

flags.refText: Smith, Logan (2023). Really Strong Features Found in Residual Stream.
flags.whyNeeded: Second of the three multilayer sparse autoencoder results cited in section 2.6 to argue the one-layer findings generalize; the residual stream setting differs from this paper's MLP-activation setting in ways that matter.

flags.refText: Cunningham, Hoagy (2023). AutoInterpretation Finds Sparse Coding Beats Alternatives.
flags.whyNeeded: Third of the generalization citations in section 2.6, and the one that compares sparse coding against alternative decomposition methods — relevant to this paper's choice of a sparse autoencoder over the architectural and classical approaches it set aside.

flags.refText: Elhage, Nelson, Hume, Tristan, Olsson, Catherine, Nanda, Neel et al. (2022). Softmax Linear Units. Transformer Circuits Thread
flags.whyNeeded: Section 2.4 cites this as the source of the few concrete examples of language model features we have, which it reads as suggestive of highly sparse variables. That empirical basis for the sparsity prior is not restated here.
